<action type="say">
Based on what you described, this usually falls under “AC not cooling well” / “performance diagnostic and maintenance,” not a full breakdown. A tech would typically check refrigerant levels, airflow, coils, blower, etc.

To point you in the right direction, I need a bit more detail:

1. Airflow & cooling:
- Is the air coming out of the vents clearly cool, just weaker?
- Or is the airflow normal but the air itself is only slightly cool / almost room temperature?

2. Filter & basics:
- When was the last time you changed or cleaned the air filter?
- Is the outdoor unit (the big fan outside) running when the AC is on?

3. Any warning signs:
- Do you hear any new odd noises (grinding, rattling, squealing, buzzing)?
- Have you ever seen ice on the indoor unit, on the refrigerant lines, or on the outdoor unit?
- Does it eventually get to the thermostat setpoint, just slower than before, or it struggles to reach it at all?

4. System details:
- Is this central AC (ducts and vents in each room) or a window / mini-split unit?
- Roughly how old is the system?

If you answer those, I can:
- Tell you what you likely need (e.g., “seasonal tune-up with diagnostic” vs “repair visit”),
- Suggest a short script you can use when contacting an HVAC company so you ask for the right thing,
- And give 2–3 safe quick checks you can do right now that might improve performance if it’s something simple (like airflow). </action>

<action type="say">
Based on what you described, this sounds like a “reduced performance” issue, not an emergency failure. The most likely culprits are airflow (dirty filter/coil, blocked vents) and age/maintenance, possibly with some early wear on components.

Here’s how I’d tackle it in order:

1) Do these simple checks first (all safe, no panels removed):
- Replace the air filter:  
  - If you can’t remember when it was changed, just swap it now.  
  - Use the same size and a **mid-range** filter (overly restrictive, high‑MERV filters can reduce airflow on older systems).  
  - After changing it, run the AC 30–60 minutes and see if airflow and cooling improve.
- Check supply & return vents:  
  - Make sure all supply vents are open and not blocked by furniture, rugs, or curtains.  
  - Find the big “return” grille(s) where air gets sucked in and check that they’re not clogged with dust; you can vacuum the grille surface.
- Outdoor unit airflow:  
  - Make sure leaves/grass/debris aren’t up against the outdoor unit; ideally you want a couple of feet of clearance around it and nothing sitting on top.  
  - Gently hose off the **outside fins** from the top down or side-to-side (power off at the thermostat first; don’t bend the fins, and don’t use a pressure washer).

If you do just those three, you’ve covered the “easy wins” for weak cooling and airflow.

2) What kind of professional visit you likely need
Given it’s 10–12 years old, hasn’t had obvious recent maintenance, and is cooling but weak, you’re in the “maintenance + diagnostic checkup” category, not necessarily a parts-replacement call yet.

When you contact an HVAC company, you can say something like:

> “My central AC is about 10–12 years old. It’s running and does eventually reach the thermostat setting, but the air feels weaker and not as cold as last year, and it runs longer to cool the house. No strange noises or ice. I’d like a **full AC tune-up with a performance diagnostic** to check airflow, refrigerant charge, and overall condition.”

That tells them:
- It’s not a no-cool emergency.
- You want more than a quick “visual inspection”; you want them to actually measure and test.

3) What a good tech should ideally do
Just so you know what to expect (and what to ask for if they only offer a “check and go”):

- Airflow and static pressure check (is the blower and ductwork moving enough air).
- Inspect and clean:
  - Indoor evaporator coil (if accessible)  
  - Blower wheel  
  - Outdoor condenser coil (more thorough cleaning than a garden hose can do)
- Electrical checks:
  - Capacitors, contactor, fan and compressor amperage.
- Refrigerant charge check:
  - Measure pressures and temperatures to see if charge and system performance are in spec.
- Thermostat & temperature drop:
  - Measure the temperature of air going into the return and coming out of a supply (a typical healthy system often has around a 16–22°F drop, though it varies).

4) When this becomes “call sooner than later”
Even if you’re not in an emergency, I would **schedule something in the near term** if:
- After changing the filter and clearing vents, it still struggles and runs almost constantly on hot days.
- You notice **ice** forming on the refrigerant lines or indoor unit.
- The air changes from “a bit cool” to almost room temperature or warm.
- You hear new buzzing, grinding, or a loud fan/compressor noise.

If you tell me:
- What filter size you have and whether you’re comfortable doing the vent/outdoor cleaning yourself, and
- Roughly where you’re located and how soon you’d *like* someone to come,

I can help you decide whether to treat this as a routine tune-up in the next week or two vs. something to get looked at sooner, and (if you want) walk you through what to ask for in a quote or booking. </action>
